drugs.name: Quinidine
drugs.mechanism: Class Ia cinchona alkaloid: blocks open Na+ channels (QRS widens) and K+ channels (QT lengthens) plus cardiac M2 receptors; also inhibits renal P-glycoprotein, raising digoxin levels.
drugs.adverseEffects: Tinnitus, headache and dizziness (like the antimalarial it comes from); antibody-mediated thrombocytopenia and hepatitis; QT prolongation with torsades; raises digoxin levels.

drugs.name: Procainamide
drugs.mechanism: Class Ia: open-state Na+ block plus K+ block (QRS and QT both lengthen), with M2 and alpha-1 blockade; N-acetylated (phase II) to an active metabolite. Used for AF with an accessory pathway.
drugs.adverseEffects: Lupus-like syndrome (arthralgia, facial rash, antihistone antibodies) in slow acetylators; hypotension from alpha-1 block; QT prolongation and torsades.

drugs.name: Disopyramide
drugs.mechanism: Class Ia Na+/K+ channel blocker with the strongest atropine-like (antimuscarinic) action of its subclass; removes the vagal brake on the AV node, so it is given with an AV-nodal blocker.
drugs.adverseEffects: Urinary retention, dry mouth and eyes, constipation, dilated pupils and tachycardia; faster AV conduction unless paired with an AV-nodal suppressant; QT prolongation.

drugs.name: Lidocaine
drugs.mechanism: Class Ib given IV: binds activated and inactivated Na+ channels and dissociates fast, acting mainly in depolarized ischemic ventricle; shortens action potential and QT. Also an amide local anesthetic.
drugs.adverseEffects: Dose-related CNS toxicity - perioral and limb paresthesias progressing to seizures; CYP450 substrate, so azole antifungals raise its level.

drugs.name: Mexiletine
drugs.mechanism: Oral Class Ib: rapid-dissociation block of inactivated Na+ channels in depolarized ventricular tissue, shortening the action potential - the by-mouth counterpart of the IV post-MI agent.
drugs.adverseEffects: GI intolerance is the main limit - nausea, vomiting, heartburn (take with food); tremor and dizziness at higher doses.

drugs.name: Phenytoin
drugs.mechanism: Antiseizure drug with Class Ib action: use-dependent block of inactivated Na+ channels that shortens the action potential; rarely used for arrhythmias today; induces hepatic CYP enzymes.
drugs.adverseEffects: Gingival overgrowth, hirsutism and nystagmus; ataxia at high levels; teratogenic; many interactions from CYP induction.

drugs.name: Flecainide / propafenone
drugs.mechanism: Class Ic: block open Na+ channels and unbind very slowly - greatest phase 0 slowing and marked QRS widening with minimal change in action potential duration; one also blocks cardiac ryanodine receptors (used in CPVT).
drugs.adverseEffects: Higher mortality after MI or with structural heart disease (CAST); proarrhythmic wide-QRS ventricular tachycardia; negative inotropy worsens heart failure.

drugs.name: Amiodarone
drugs.mechanism: Iodinated Class III with broad action: K+, Na+ and Ca2+ channel block plus alpha and beta blockade; half-life about 60 days; CYP3A4 substrate that inhibits P450, raising digoxin, warfarin and statin levels.
drugs.adverseEffects: Pulmonary fibrosis (interstitial inflammation, type II pneumocyte hyperplasia), hypo- or hyperthyroidism, hepatotoxic metabolite, corneal deposits, blue-gray skin; get baseline chest X-ray, LFTs and thyroid panel.

drugs.name: Dronedarone
drugs.mechanism: Non-iodinated analogue of the broad-spectrum Class III drug: blocks K+, Na+ and Ca2+ channels with some beta and alpha blockade, but carries no iodine atoms; used to keep sinus rhythm in AF.
drugs.adverseEffects: Much less thyroid, corneal and skin toxicity than its iodinated parent; QT prolongation; raises mortality in advanced or recently decompensated HF and in permanent AF; liver injury.

drugs.name: Sotalol
drugs.mechanism: Nonselective beta blocker (Class II) that also blocks delayed-rectifier K+ channels (Class III), prolonging the action potential and QT; renally cleared; used for atrial fibrillation.
drugs.adverseEffects: Dose-related QT prolongation and torsades, worst at slow rates, plus beta-2 effects - wheezing in COPD or asthma - and bradycardia; dose by renal function.

drugs.name: Dofetilide / ibutilide
drugs.mechanism: Pure Class III: block the rapid delayed-rectifier K+ current, delaying phase 3 without touching phase 0 or resting potential; reverse use-dependent; one oral, one IV, for AF and atrial flutter.
drugs.adverseEffects: Marked QT prolongation and torsades with no beta-blocker effects; ECG monitoring for at least 4 hours after the IV infusion, or about 3 days in hospital while the oral agent is started and dosed to renal function.

drugs.name: Verapamil / diltiazem
drugs.mechanism: Class IV: L-type Ca2+ channel block in SA/AV node and myocardium as well as arterioles (one agent more cardiac than the other) - flatter phase 4, longer AV-nodal refractory period, less contractility.
drugs.adverseEffects: Bradycardia and AV block, hypotension without reflex tachycardia, constipation, raised digoxin levels; contraindicated in HFrEF and pre-excited AF; overdose raises glucose (IV calcium, insulin).

drugs.name: Adenosine
drugs.mechanism: Agonist at A1 (Gi) receptors in SA and AV nodes, causing transient AV block that terminates PSVT; half-life about 5 seconds, given by rapid IV push; antagonized by methylxanthines.
drugs.adverseEffects: Seconds-long flushing and hypotension (A2-Gs vasodilation), chest tightness and wheeze (A2B-Gq bronchoconstriction), a brief pause; blunted by theophylline and caffeine.

drugs.name: Magnesium sulfate
drugs.mechanism: IV divalent cation that blocks Ca2+ influx into the cytosol, suppressing early and delayed afterdepolarizations - first line for torsades and for digitalis-induced arrhythmias, even with a normal serum level.
drugs.adverseEffects: Flushing and hypotension during infusion; at high serum levels, loss of deep tendon reflexes, respiratory depression, bradycardia and heart block (reverse with IV calcium); caution in renal failure.

drugs.name: Digoxin
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits myocyte Na+/K+-ATPase, so the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger extrudes less Ca2+ (positive inotropy); also raises vagal tone (slower SA rate, AV-nodal block, long PR). Long half-life, narrow therapeutic index.
drugs.adverseEffects: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea; yellow vision and halos; gynecomastia; delayed-afterdepolarization arrhythmias worsened by low K+ or Mg2+, high Ca2+, renal failure, verapamil, quinidine, amiodarone; antidote Fab fragments.

drugs.name: Ivabradine
drugs.mechanism: Selective block of the If (funny) current in SA-node pacemaker cells: slows heart rate without changing contractility, conduction or action potential duration; for HF or stable angina when a beta blocker cannot be used.
drugs.adverseEffects: Bradycardia (watch for AV block); transient bright spots in the visual field from retinal Ih channel block; avoid in pregnancy; CYP3A4 inhibitors such as grapefruit raise levels.

drugs.name: Metoprolol / atenolol / bisoprolol
drugs.mechanism: Beta-1 selective antagonists used orally for long-term therapy with no partial agonist or vasodilator action: flatten phase 4 in SA/AV node, lower contractility and renin release (Class II); two of the three cut mortality in HFrEF.
drugs.adverseEffects: AV block and bradycardia are the main concern; fatigue; rebound tachycardia or angina if stopped abruptly; spare the airways at usual doses but can mask hypoglycemia.

drugs.name: Propranolol / nadolol / timolol
drugs.mechanism: Nonselective beta-1 and beta-2 antagonists without partial agonism or alpha block: slow SA/AV node and contractility, and block hepatic glycogenolysis and bronchial and vascular beta-2 relaxation; rate control in thyroid storm.
drugs.adverseEffects: Bronchospasm in asthma or COPD, hypoglycemia with blunted warning signs, worse claudication in PVD, bradycardia; overdose gives bradycardia, AV block, hypotension, low glucose - treat with glucagon.

drugs.name: Labetalol / carvedilol
drugs.mechanism: Combined alpha-1 and nonselective beta antagonists: alpha block dilates arterioles while beta block prevents reflex tachycardia; one is an HFrEF survival drug with antioxidant action, the other treats hypertension in pregnancy.
drugs.adverseEffects: Orthostatic hypotension and dizziness from alpha-1 block, bradycardia, fatigue, fluid retention while titrating in HF; bronchospasm possible because beta-2 is blocked too.

drugs.name: Pindolol / acebutolol
drugs.mechanism: Beta blockers with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity - partial agonists, one nonselective and one beta-1 selective: block catecholamine surges yet stimulate the receptor at rest, so resting heart rate falls little.
drugs.adverseEffects: Can worsen angina, post-MI ischemia and heart failure by raising cardiac workload - avoid in those patients; less resting bradycardia than other agents of the class.

drugs.name: Esmolol
drugs.mechanism: IV beta-1 selective antagonist hydrolyzed by red-cell esterases; half-life about 9 minutes, so the effect is titratable and ends minutes after stopping - acute rate control (e.g. arrhythmia from theophylline overdose).
drugs.adverseEffects: Hypotension and bradycardia that resolve within minutes of stopping the infusion; irritation or phlebitis at the infusion site.

drugs.name: Nebivolol
drugs.mechanism: Highly beta-1 selective antagonist that also stimulates endothelial nitric oxide release, adding vasodilation without any alpha blockade.
drugs.adverseEffects: Fatigue, bradycardia, headache and dizziness; erectile dysfunction and bronchospasm are less common than with older beta blockers, thanks to high beta-1 selectivity plus NO release.

drugs.name: Nitroglycerin / isosorbide dinitrate / isosorbide mononitrate
drugs.mechanism: Bioactivated by glutathione-S-transferase and a mitochondrial aldehyde enzyme to release NO -> guanylyl cyclase -> cGMP -> smooth-muscle relaxation, mainly venous: preload and O2 demand fall; sublingual route skips first pass.
drugs.adverseEffects: Throbbing headache, orthostatic hypotension with reflex tachycardia, salt and water retention; tolerance with continuous use (needs an 8- to 12-hour drug-free interval each day); severe hypotension with PDE5 inhibitors.

drugs.name: Nitroprusside
drugs.mechanism: Short-acting IV NO donor (an iron-cyanide complex) that dilates arterioles and venules equally, lowering afterload and preload at once - for hypertensive emergency and acute HF.
drugs.adverseEffects: Cyanide and its metabolite thiocyanate accumulate with high doses, long infusions or renal impairment - confusion, flushed pink skin, dyspnea, lactic acidosis - treated with hydroxocobalamin or sodium thiosulfate; profound hypotension.

drugs.name: Ranolazine
drugs.mechanism: Blocks the late inward Na+ current in myocytes, so less Ca2+ enters via the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger and wall tension and O2 use fall without lowering heart rate or BP; chronic angina, not first line.
drugs.adverseEffects: QT prolongation (partial K+ channel block), constipation, nausea, dizziness; levels and QT risk rise with CYP3A inhibitors such as azole antifungals and grapefruit.

drugs.name: Trimetazidine
drugs.mechanism: Metabolic modulator: inhibits myocardial fatty-acid oxidation, shifting the ischemic heart to glucose oxidation (more ATP per O2 used); not approved in the US.
drugs.adverseEffects: New or worsened parkinsonian symptoms - tremor, rigidity, gait disturbance - the safety concern behind its lack of US approval.

drugs.name: Aspirin
drugs.mechanism: Irreversibly acetylates COX-1 and COX-2; anucleate platelets cannot make new enzyme, so TXA2 is lost for their 7-10 day life, while endothelium recovers and keeps making prostacyclin at low dose.
drugs.adverseEffects: GI bleeding (loss of protective prostaglandins), bronchospasm from LOX shunting, Reye syndrome in children; overdose: respiratory alkalosis then metabolic acidosis (uncoupling) - give bicarbonate.

drugs.name: Clopidogrel
drugs.mechanism: Oral prodrug activated by hepatic CYP2C19; the active metabolite irreversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor; given with aspirin after stenting and for unstable angina or NSTEMI.
drugs.adverseEffects: Bleeding (gums, stool); fails in CYP2C19 loss-of-function carriers or with omeprazole (2C19 inhibition) - change the PPI or switch to a direct-acting agent.

drugs.name: Ticlopidine
drugs.mechanism: The original oral ADP (P2Y12) receptor blocker: an irreversible prodrug, largely abandoned because of its blood-count toxicity.
drugs.adverseEffects: Neutropenia appearing weeks into therapy (sore throat, fever, flu-like illness) - needs CBC monitoring; also TTP and bleeding.

drugs.name: Prasugrel
drugs.mechanism: Oral irreversible P2Y12 prodrug whose activation does not depend on CYP2C19, so platelet inhibition is faster, stronger and more consistent than with the 2C19-activated agent; ACS with PCI.
drugs.adverseEffects: More bleeding than the 2C19-activated agent; contraindicated after a prior stroke or TIA (intracranial bleeding) and generally avoided at age 75 or older.

drugs.name: Ticagrelor
drugs.mechanism: Oral, direct-acting (not a prodrug), reversible P2Y12 antagonist - needs no hepatic activation, so it still works when CYP2C19 is impaired; taken twice daily with aspirin after ACS or PCI.
drugs.adverseEffects: Bleeding (more than the 2C19-activated agent) and dyspnea; bradyarrhythmias and ventricular pauses; raised uric acid; costlier; high-dose aspirin blunts its benefit.

drugs.name: Cangrelor
drugs.mechanism: IV direct-acting, reversible P2Y12 antagonist: no first-pass metabolism, onset within minutes and platelet function back about an hour after the infusion stops - used around PCI.
drugs.adverseEffects: Bleeding that wears off within about an hour of stopping the IV infusion, which makes it the bridge when surgery may follow.

drugs.name: Abciximab / eptifibatide / tirofiban
drugs.mechanism: Block platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa so fibrinogen cannot cross-link platelets (the final common step); the antibody is off the US market, the two small molecules are reversible, short-acting continuous infusions.
drugs.adverseEffects: Bleeding that reproduces an inherited lack of the platelet fibrinogen receptor (Glanzmann); thrombocytopenia; kept for high thrombus risk, aspirin allergy or ADP-blocker intolerance.

drugs.name: Cilostazol
drugs.mechanism: PDE3 inhibitor in platelets and arterial smooth muscle: raises cAMP, inhibiting aggregation and dilating arteries and enhancing prostacyclin action; lengthens walking distance in intermittent claudication.
drugs.adverseEffects: Headache, diarrhea, palpitations and tachycardia; contraindicated in heart failure of any severity (oral PDE3 inhibition raised mortality); CYP3A4 and 2C19 inhibitors raise levels.

drugs.name: Dipyridamole
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits platelet phosphodiesterase and blocks cellular adenosine reuptake, raising cAMP and local adenosine - coronary vasodilation used for pharmacologic stress testing; antiplatelet when paired with aspirin.
drugs.adverseEffects: Worsened angina from coronary steal (dilates normal beds and diverts flow from ischemic ones); headache, flushing, dizziness, hypotension; effects reversed by aminophylline.

drugs.name: Amlodipine / felodipine / nifedipine
drugs.mechanism: Block L-type Ca2+ channels in arteriolar smooth muscle only (Ca2+-calmodulin-MLCK chain), lowering TPR and afterload with little direct SA/AV-node effect; two are once daily, one treats hypertension in pregnancy.
drugs.adverseEffects: Reflex tachycardia (baroreceptor), flushing, headache, dizziness, ankle edema from arteriolar dilation, gingival overgrowth; grapefruit (CYP3A4) raises levels and worsens these effects.

drugs.name: ACE inhibitors (lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril, captopril)
drugs.mechanism: Block the enzyme that converts angiotensin I to II and also degrades bradykinin: less vasoconstriction, aldosterone and ADH; lower preload and afterload, less remodeling; efferent dilation protects diabetic kidneys.
drugs.adverseEffects: Bradykinin dry cough (the usual reason to switch to an AT1 blocker) and angioedema, a risk shared with the neprilysin combination; hyperkalemia; first-dose hypotension; renal failure in bilateral renal artery stenosis; fetal renal toxicity.

drugs.name: ARBs (losartan, valsartan, candesartan)
drugs.mechanism: Block angiotensin II at the AT1 receptor while leaving bradykinin breakdown intact: lower afterload, preload, aldosterone and remodeling - the standard replacement when the converting-enzyme blocker causes cough.
drugs.adverseEffects: No bradykinin cough - patients with ACE-inhibitor cough are switched to it - and angioedema is rare; still hyperkalemia, first-dose dizziness, fetal kidney toxicity, renal failure with bilateral renal artery stenosis.

drugs.name: Aliskiren
drugs.mechanism: Direct renin inhibitor: blocks conversion of angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, so angiotensin II and aldosterone both fall; used only after the other RAAS blockers fail.
drugs.adverseEffects: Hyperkalemia and hypotension like other RAAS blockers; diarrhea; fetal toxicity; do not combine with an ACE inhibitor or AT1 blocker in diabetes (renal failure, hyperkalemia).

drugs.name: Sacubitril-valsartan
drugs.mechanism: Combination of a prodrug that inhibits neprilysin, so natriuretic peptides persist (natriuresis, vasodilation), with an AT1 receptor blocker; improves survival and cuts hospitalizations in HFrEF.
drugs.adverseEffects: Hypotension, hyperkalemia, renal dysfunction; angioedema - never start within 36 hours of an ACE inhibitor, because neprilysin also breaks down bradykinin.

drugs.name: Spironolactone
drugs.mechanism: Steroidal competitive antagonist of the aldosterone (mineralocorticoid) receptor in collecting-duct principal cells that also blocks androgen receptors; used in HF, hyperaldosteronism, acne and hirsutism.
drugs.adverseEffects: Gynecomastia, impotence and menstrual changes (anti-androgen); hyperkalemia with metabolic acidosis, worse with ACEi/ARB, NSAIDs or K+ supplements - check K+ periodically.

drugs.name: Eplerenone / finerenone
drugs.mechanism: Selective mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists with little androgen or progesterone receptor binding; the newer one is nonsteroidal, the most selective, and slows progression of chronic kidney disease.
drugs.adverseEffects: Hyperkalemia and acidosis (monitor K+, especially with ACEi/ARB or NSAIDs) without gynecomastia or impotence - the switch when breast enlargement appears on the older agent; costlier.

drugs.name: Furosemide / bumetanide / torsemide
drugs.mechanism: Sulfonamide 'high-ceiling' diuretics: block the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter in the thick ascending limb, losing the lumen-positive potential so Ca2+ and Mg2+ are wasted; raise PGE2 and venodilate, cutting preload.
drugs.adverseEffects: Ototoxicity (additive with aminoglycosides, cisplatin, vancomycin), hypokalemic alkalosis, low Mg2+ and Ca2+, hyperuricemia, sulfa allergy; NSAIDs blunt the effect; low K+ potentiates digoxin.

drugs.name: Ethacrynic acid
drugs.mechanism: Thick-ascending-limb Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter blocker that is not a sulfonamide (contains no sulfur) - the option when a patient with sulfa allergy needs a high-ceiling diuretic.
drugs.adverseEffects: The most ototoxic drug of its class (hearing loss, tinnitus); hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hyperuricemia, GI upset; no cross-reaction in sulfa-allergic patients.

drugs.name: Hydrochlorothiazide / chlorthalidone / indapamide
drugs.mechanism: Block the Na+/Cl- cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule and enhance Ca2+ reabsorption there; volume contraction paradoxically lowers urine output in nephrogenic DI; used for HTN, HF and Ca2+ stones.
drugs.adverseEffects: Hyperglycemia, hyperlipidemia, hyperuricemia, hypercalcemia, hyponatremia, hypokalemic alkalosis; sulfa allergy, photosensitivity; raise lithium levels; low K+ potentiates digoxin.

drugs.name: SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, canagliflozin)
drugs.mechanism: Block Na+-glucose cotransport in the proximal tubule: glycosuria plus natriuresis and osmotic diuresis lower preload and afterload; cut HF hospitalization and CV death in HFrEF and HFpEF; A1c falls up to about 1%.
drugs.adverseEffects: UTIs and genital yeast infections (glucose in the urine), volume depletion, euglycemic ketoacidosis; avoid when creatinine clearance is below about 20-30 mL/min.

drugs.name: Hydralazine
drugs.mechanism: Direct arteriolar dilator (raises smooth-muscle cGMP) that lowers afterload with little venous effect; hepatically acetylated; paired with a venodilating NO donor for HFrEF survival; IV for severe preeclampsia.
drugs.adverseEffects: Lupus-like syndrome in slow acetylators; reflex tachycardia (can provoke angina) and salt and water retention, so it often needs a beta blocker and a diuretic; headache, flushing.

drugs.name: Dobutamine
drugs.mechanism: Direct beta-1 agonist (Gs -> adenylyl cyclase -> cAMP -> PKA -> Ca2+ entry) that raises contractility with mild vasodilation; IV for acute decompensated HF and cardiogenic shock; also a stress-test agent.
drugs.adverseEffects: Tachycardia, ventricular ectopy and arrhythmias, angina from higher O2 demand, blood pressure swings; tolerance after 48-72 hours of infusion.

drugs.name: Milrinone
drugs.mechanism: IV PDE3 inhibitor in myocardium and vascular smooth muscle: stops cAMP breakdown without acting on any receptor, so contractility rises while arterioles and veins dilate (inodilator); acute decompensated HF.
drugs.adverseEffects: Hypotension from vasodilation, atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, headache; accumulates in renal impairment (dose by renal function); long-term oral PDE3 inhibition raised HF mortality.

drugs.name: Dopamine
drugs.mechanism: Dose-dependent agonist: low dose D1 (renal and splanchnic vasodilation, preserves GFR and renal blood flow), medium dose beta-1 (inotropy), high dose alpha-1 (vasoconstriction); IV in acute HF and shock.
drugs.adverseEffects: Tachyarrhythmias; intense vasoconstriction with limb ischemia at high doses; tissue necrosis if it extravasates (infiltrate phentolamine); nausea and vomiting.

drugs.name: Vericiguat
drugs.mechanism: Oral stimulator of soluble guanylyl cyclase that raises cGMP independent of nitric oxide (and sensitizes the enzyme to NO); cuts HF hospitalization after a worsening episode of HFrEF.
drugs.adverseEffects: Hypotension, headache, dizziness, reflex tachycardia; never combine with NO donors or PDE5 inhibitors; no tolerance, so no drug-free interval is needed; embryo-fetal toxicity.

drugs.name: Nesiritide
drugs.mechanism: Recombinant B-type natriuretic peptide: activates the membrane-bound (particulate) guanylyl cyclase receptor, raising cGMP for venous and arterial dilation plus natriuresis; formerly given IV in acute decompensated HF.
drugs.adverseEffects: Hypotension and worsening renal function - kidney harm without a survival benefit is why it was abandoned.

drugs.name: Conivaptan
drugs.mechanism: IV antagonist of vasopressin V1a receptors (vascular - lowers PVR) and V2 receptors (collecting duct - fewer aquaporins, free-water excretion); raises serum Na+ in euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia.
drugs.adverseEffects: Overly rapid Na+ correction risks osmotic demyelination; infusion-site phlebitis; hypotension; strong CYP3A4 inhibitor with many interactions.

drugs.name: Semaglutide
drugs.mechanism: GLP-1 receptor agonist: glucose-dependent insulin release, less glucagon, slower gastric emptying and central appetite suppression; the weight loss helps obesity-related HF (HFpEF).
drugs.adverseEffects: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea; pancreatitis and gallbladder disease; thyroid C-cell tumor warning (avoid with medullary thyroid cancer or MEN2); hypoglycemia mainly with insulin or sulfonylureas.

drugs.name: Statins (atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, simvastatin, pravastatin)
drugs.mechanism: Competitive inhibitors of HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis; hepatocytes up-regulate LDL receptors and LDL falls 25% to 50% or more, dose-dependent; proven to cut cardiac deaths.
drugs.adverseEffects: Myalgia, myopathy and rhabdomyolysis (check CK; possible CoQ10 depletion), raised aminotransferases (stop if >3x ULN), slight glucose rise; levels rise with azoles, macrolides, grapefruit; no pregnancy.

drugs.name: Cholestyramine / colestipol / colesevelam
drugs.mechanism: Non-absorbed resins that bind bile acids in the gut and break enterohepatic recirculation; the liver up-regulates 7-alpha-hydroxylase and LDL receptors to make new bile acids, so LDL falls about 30%.
drugs.adverseEffects: Bloating, constipation, nausea; bind thyroxine, digoxin, warfarin, thiazides, estrogens and vitamins A, D, E, K - space doses several hours apart; acceptable in pregnancy and children.

drugs.name: Niacin
drugs.mechanism: Inhibits lipolysis in adipocytes, so less free fatty acid reaches the liver - less TG and VLDL secretion and lower LDL; gives the largest HDL rise of any lipid drug (30-40%).
drugs.adverseEffects: Prostaglandin-mediated flushing and itching (pretreat with aspirin or use slow release), hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia and gout, worsened peptic ulcer, myositis with a statin; avoid in pregnancy.

drugs.name: Gemfibrozil / fenofibrate
drugs.mechanism: Synthetic PPAR-alpha ligands: change gene transcription to raise lipoprotein lipase (ApoC-II up, ApoC-III down) and hepatic fatty-acid oxidation, degrading VLDL - TG fall about 35%; also suppress 7-alpha-hydroxylase.
drugs.adverseEffects: Cholesterol gallstones (less bile acid made, bile relatively rich in cholesterol); myopathy and rhabdomyolysis, especially combined with a statin, with renal injury.

drugs.name: Ezetimibe
drugs.mechanism: Blocks the Niemann-Pick C1-Like 1 (NPC1L1) sterol transporter at the small-intestine brush border, cutting cholesterol absorption into chylomicrons; adds about 25% LDL lowering to a statin.
drugs.adverseEffects: Generally mild - GI upset and a small rise in liver enzymes when combined with a statin (check LFTs); occasional muscle aches.

drugs.name: Alirocumab / evolocumab
drugs.mechanism: Monoclonal antibodies that bind circulating PCSK9 protein so it cannot send LDL receptors to lysosomes; receptors recycle and LDL and ApoB-100 drop sharply; SQ every 2 weeks or monthly on top of a maximal statin.
drugs.adverseEffects: Injection-site reactions (cold compress, topical hydrocortisone), hypersensitivity, myalgia with a statin; no proven cognitive harm since they do not cross the blood-brain barrier; expensive.

drugs.name: Inclisiran
drugs.mechanism: Small interfering RNA taken up by hepatocytes that degrades PCSK9 mRNA, so the protein is never made and LDL receptors rise; SQ injection only twice a year.
drugs.adverseEffects: Mild injection-site reactions, arthralgia and bronchitis; being a liver-targeted siRNA rather than an antibody, systemic hypersensitivity is uncommon; clinic-given twice yearly.

drugs.name: Lomitapide
drugs.mechanism: Oral inhibitor of microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP), blocking assembly of ApoB-48 chylomicrons in gut and ApoB-100 VLDL in liver; for homozygous FH (LDL > 500 mg/dL) despite PCSK9-directed therapy.
drugs.adverseEffects: Hepatotoxicity from hepatic fat accumulation with raised aminotransferases (restricted REMS program), GI upset and steatorrhea, pregnancy category X, CYP3A4 interactions, more toxicity with statins.

drugs.name: Omega-3 fatty acids (EPA/DHA, icosapent ethyl)
drugs.mechanism: Long-chain polyunsaturated lipids acting as PPAR-alpha agonists, stimulating lipoprotein lipase to clear VLDL; the purified single-component product also lowers ApoC-III; antithrombotic (less TXA2, more prostacyclin).
drugs.adverseEffects: Bleeding and easy bruising, worse with aspirin, clopidogrel or anticoagulants; fishy aftertaste, belching and GI upset; the purified prescription product raises atrial fibrillation risk.

drugs.name: Bempedoic acid
drugs.mechanism: Oral prodrug activated in liver but not muscle; inhibits ATP citrate lyase upstream of HMG-CoA reductase, cutting cytosolic acetyl-CoA for cholesterol synthesis; LDL receptors rise; for statin-intolerant patients.
drugs.adverseEffects: Hyperuricemia and gout (competes at the renal urate transporter), tendon rupture (older adults, glucocorticoid or fluoroquinolone users); less myopathy than HMG-CoA reductase blockers.

drugs.name: Evinacumab
drugs.mechanism: Monoclonal antibody against angiopoietin-like protein 3 (ANGPTL3), lifting its brake on lipoprotein lipase and endothelial lipase; lowers LDL without needing LDL receptors - monthly IV infusion for homozygous FH.
drugs.adverseEffects: Infusion reactions and anaphylaxis - given in a monitored facility and can be premedicated; nasopharyngitis and flu-like symptoms; embryo-fetal toxicity.
